headline: WFC drops 3.1% and health care slides as JPMorgan's results leave stocks flat before CPI

summary.text: SPY finished 0.01% lower on the first big-bank earnings day, while WFC fell 3.1% and health care lost 1.35%. JPMorgan's and UnitedHealth's results cannot be called beats or misses because the free data's two consensus figures differ. Tomorrow's CPI, set against August's 0.4% rise, is the open question.

paragraphs.text: Big-bank earnings got under way and the S&P 500 barely moved, with SPY closing 0.01% lower. JPMorgan Chase reported earnings per share of $5.75 and its shares fell 0.86%. The feed carries two consensus figures, $5.715 and $5.94, so Optic does not call that a beat or a miss.

The sharper moves were underneath. WFC dropped 3.1% on 1.74 times its usual volume, and the health care fund (XLV) lost 1.35% even though UnitedHealth, which also reported, slipped only 0.2%. The data shows these moves, not their causes.

The tension is tomorrow at 8:30 a.m. Eastern, when the next consumer price index arrives. The last reading, for August and published in September, showed prices up 0.4% on the month. WSJ wrote that bank results failed to quash worries about inflation and Fed rate hikes, which puts the weight on that print.

items.label: WFC shares, 13 October session
items.text: From $83.32, against a typical daily move of 1.18%. Nothing in the evidence explains it.

items.label: Health care (XLV), 13 October session
items.text: Against a typical 0.58% day. UNH fell only 0.2%, so the drop came from elsewhere; biotech (XBI) fell 3.04%.

items.label: US dollar index, day
items.text: Bigger than its typical 0.26% day. Gold edged up 0.16%, small beside its typical 0.77%, so the dollar-gold link is mixed.

items.label: High-yield bonds (HYG), day
items.text: Beyond its typical 0.21% day while stocks were flat. Junk bonds are repaid only if companies stay solvent, so credit leaned more cautious than shares; the relationship is mixed.

items.label: JPM EPS, quarter reported 13 October
items.text: Consensus figures of $5.715 and $5.94 differ, so no call. Revenue and guidance are not in the free data.

items.label: UNH EPS, quarter reported 13 October
items.text: Consensus figures of $2.17 and $4.14 are far apart, so no call.

paragraphs.text: Bank results reflect the households and businesses banks lend to, but one bank's EPS is thin evidence. The labour cross-check disagrees with itself: jobless claims were a low 197,000 in the week to 3 October, while September payrolls grew only 29,000, against 133,000 in August, and unemployment rose to 4.2%.

Rates are why CPI carries weight. The 10-year yield eased 2.3 basis points to 5.217%. WSJ tied the retreat partly to lower Brent crude, though WTI rose 1.06%. New York Fed President John Williams sees one more hike in 2026 and none in 2027, which CNBC called at odds with traders, while the IMF warned yields could spike in a disorderly way.

Oil is the relationship today's figures fit: WTI rose 1.06% and the energy fund (XLE) 1.8%, as you would expect when oil is producers' revenue. Consistent, not proof. Breadth was split, with 5 of 11 sector funds up, but over five sessions the equal-weight S&P 500 has beaten the cap-weighted index by 0.6 percentage points, so recent softness has sat in the biggest names.

sections.title: The good, the bad and the unresolved

good.text: Energy led, with oil and gas producers (XOP) up 2.85%. OPEC's 2.6 million barrels a day of projected 2027 demand growth is a forecast, not a demonstrated cause.
The average stock held up: RSP rose 0.05%.

bad.text: MU fell 3.62% and is down 8.83% over five sessions; MarketWatch described chips' worst stretch in 16 months.
Small caps (IWM) fell 0.43% and sit 4.82% below their 50-day average.

unresolved.text: Gold miners (GDX) fell 1.46% while gold rose 0.16%.

items.text: Bank of America reports tomorrow against a $1.10 EPS consensus, after the Financial Times reported a $1.2bn fine over money-laundering failures. CNBC and WSJ carried the same story: wider coverage, not independent confirmation.
V rose 1.74% to $396.06, above its 20-day high of $391.81.
MU, at $953.19, is still 34.52% above its 200-day average, so the long trend and the recent selling tell different stories.
Homebuilders (ITB) rose 0.77% on 2.42 times normal volume but sit 12.63% below their 200-day average, with the 30-year mortgage rate at 7.4% in the week of 8 October.

paragraphs.text: On daily bars to 13 October, SPY closed at 778.01, above its 50-day average of 768.6 and inside its 20-day range of 749.6 to 781.62, on 0.58 times normal volume. QQQ closed at 743.57, below its 20-day high of 762.86.

The VIX rose 0.43 points to 15.27. SPY's at-the-money straddle prices about 0.52% either way to the 14 October expiry, which covers CPI day, close to SPY's typical 0.48% day; it is a price, not a forecast. QQQ prices 0.86% to that expiry. To the 13 November expiry, SPY prices 2.88% and QQQ 4.29%. These are Optic's estimates from delayed quotes.

items.text: If hotter than August's 0.4%, the case for rates staying high strengthens, and yields would show it first; if cooler, pressure on yields eases, and watch whether the dollar falls with them.
Above the $1.10 consensus would give JPM's ambiguous read company; below, watch whether bank shares extend WFC's weakness.

items.what: Producer Price Index and TSM results
items.text: PPI hotter than August's 0.4% would add to yield pressure; cooler would ease it. TSM above its $4.52 consensus would test the AI-fatigue story; below would fit chips' recent weakness.

items.what: Import prices and monthly options expiry
items.text: Import prices hotter than the previous 0.67% would lean on yields; cooler would ease them. At expiry, strike-related hedging ends: a pinned index may loosen, a trending one may barely notice.
Read CPI against August's 0.4% and watch the 10-year yield for the first reaction.
Treat bank results as evidence about their own customers; BAC adds a second data point.
Track whether WFC's drop and health care's slide extend or fade.
Watch whether credit keeps leaning more cautious than stocks, and whether TSM on Thursday steadies chips.

relationships.claim: A stronger dollar usually weighs on gold, which is priced in dollars
relationships.mechanism: Gold costs more in other currencies when the dollar rises, which can reduce demand.
relationships.note: Dollar -0.36%, gold +0.16%. Real yields, central-bank buying and safe-haven demand also move gold.

relationships.claim: Oil prices feed into inflation expectations and energy company profits

relationships.claim: Credit and stocks usually agree about risk

relationships.claim: A move carried by most sectors says more than one carried by a few
relationships.mechanism: When the index moves on a handful of large companies, the average stock can be doing something different.

relationships.claim: Bank results are evidence about their own customers' borrowing and repayment

evidence.label: Consumer Price Index
evidence.method: No consensus forecast: Optic does not carry surveyed expectations, so a release is compared with its own previous reading.

compare.headline: CPI for all items increases 0.4% in August; gasoline rises

evidence.text: The inflation print the Fed's 2% mandate is written against. Rate expectations for the next two meetings usually reset within seconds of the release, which is why it moves the whole index and not just rate-sensitive sectors. Core (stripping food and energy) is what gets traded; the headline number is noisier because of petrol.

evidence.label: Producer Price Index
evidence.method: No consensus forecast: Optic does not carry surveyed expectations, so a release is compared with its own previous reading.

compare.headline: PPI for final demand moves up 0.4% in August; goods advance 1.1%, services rise 0.1%

evidence.text: Prices at the factory gate, before anything reaches a shop shelf. Read as a leading indicator for CPI and as a direct read on margins: a producer absorbing higher input costs is a producer with a thinner margin next quarter.

evidence.label: U.S. Import and Export Price Indexes
evidence.method: No consensus forecast: Optic does not carry surveyed expectations, so a release is compared with its own previous reading.
evidence.text: Traded-goods prices, which is where the dollar shows up in inflation. A strong dollar makes imports cheaper and quietly does some of the Fed's work; a weak one does the opposite. Mostly a second-order read on CPI.

evidence.label: CFTC Commitments of Traders
evidence.method: No consensus forecast: Optic does not carry surveyed expectations, so a release is compared with its own previous reading.
evidence.text: Weekly positioning: how large speculators and commercial hedgers are actually placed across futures. It is a Tuesday snapshot published on Friday, so it is history, not a signal. Its use is spotting a crowded trade, where an extreme reading means the marginal buyer has already bought.

evidence.label: Monthly options expiry
evidence.method: No consensus forecast: Optic does not carry surveyed expectations, so a release is compared with its own previous reading.
evidence.text: Standard equity and index options expire. The dealer hedging tied to those strikes stops existing at the close, so levels that have been acting like a magnet or a ceiling all month simply stop doing so.

evidence.label: VIX futures and options settlement
evidence.method: No consensus forecast: Optic does not carry surveyed expectations, so a release is compared with its own previous reading.
evidence.text: VIX settles against a special opening auction of SPX options, not against a close, and it lands on a Wednesday rather than with equity opex. A distinction routinely missed. Hedges rolled around this date can move implied volatility without the index itself doing much.

evidence.label: Fed funds futures: change priced over November 2026
evidence.source: CME 30-day fed funds futures (ZQ=F) via Yahoo; Optic's arithmetic
evidence.method: No meeting falls inside November, the delivery month of the front contract, so this is the move priced into that month's average rather than the odds on a decision.
